title: Constant expressions
recap: A constant expression is an expression whose literals, variables, operators, and function calls are all evaluatable at compile time. A non-const variable cannot be used in a constant expression even when its initializer is a literal.

A const integral variable initialized by a constant expression is usable in constant expressions. Modern code generally prefers constexpr when a value is intended to be a compile-time constant, and static_assert requires a constant-expression condition.
objectives: Make a const int usable in a constant expression.
Initialize a constexpr int from compile-time operands.
Use static_assert to verify a calculated invariant during compilation.
Distinguish a constant initializer from a variable that is usable in constant expressions.
warnings: A literal initializer does not make a non-const variable usable in a constant expression.
A constexpr variable must have a constant-expression initializer.
Do not replace the calculated capacity with the expected numeric result.
challenge: Repair the declarations so rows is a const int usable in constant expressions, seatsPerRow is explicitly constexpr, and capacity is a constexpr product of those two variables. Retain the static_assert that verifies 24 seats and print the calculated capacity in a deterministic no-input run.
hints: The literal 4 is a constant expression, but the current non-const rows variable is not usable in one.
Add const to the integral rows declaration; a const integral variable with a constant-expression initializer is usable at compile time.
Keep capacity constexpr and initialized with rows * seatsPerRow so static_assert can evaluate the product during compilation.
